issues.legal_issue: A confiscation order cannot be sustained when the authority relies on a confiscation power that was omitted before the order was made and the pending proceeding was not saved by the governing law.
material_facts: Confiscation proceedings against the company began under a rule that authorized confiscation of land, buildings, plant and machinery.
That rule was omitted before the final confiscation orders were made.
The later rules did not restore the power to confiscate those immovable and fixed assets; their vesting provisions referred to confiscated goods.
The bank challenged the confiscation orders, which were made after it had taken security over the company’s assets.
issues.conclusion: The pending confiscation proceedings were not saved, and the confiscation orders were without jurisdiction and were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 38A(c) and (e) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, savings for accrued liabilities and pending proceedings apply only unless a different legislative intention appears. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 does not save proceedings following omission of a rule. Applying the Constitution Bench ruling in Kolhapur Canesugar Works Ltd. v. Union of India, pending proceedings lapse when the omitted rule is not continued by the replacement rules or another applicable saving provision. The Court approved the reasoning in Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. District Magistrate that the later rules did not authorize confiscation of land and other immovable assets.

rule.if: challenge_to_confiscation_order and proceeding_started_under_prior_rule and rule_omitted_before_final_order and replacement_rules_do_not_retain_immovable_asset_confiscation and no_applicable_saving_preserves_proceeding

predicates.challenge_to_confiscation_order: A party challenges an administrative order confiscating business assets.
predicates.proceeding_started_under_prior_rule: The authority began the confiscation proceeding under a rule that then authorized the relevant confiscation.
predicates.rule_omitted_before_final_order: The rule supplying the asserted confiscation power was omitted before the authority made its final order.
predicates.replacement_rules_do_not_retain_immovabl: The rules replacing the omitted rule do not retain authority to confiscate the relevant immovable or fixed assets.
predicates.no_applicable_saving_preserves_proceedin: No applicable saving provision preserves the pending proceeding in light of the legislative intent shown by the replacement rules.
predicates.confiscation_order_invalid: The confiscation order is invalid for lack of authority.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a confiscation order made after the governing power was omitted, and the replacement rules and applicable savings do not preserve that power or proceeding, the order is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A secured creditor’s claim to secured assets has priority over government excise dues when the applicable law gives the secured creditor priority and the excise claim has no applicable first charge.
material_facts: The company mortgaged and hypothecated its assets to a consortium of banks to secure credit facilities.
The excise department claimed duties and penalties from the company in relation to the same assets.
The applicable excise law did not give the department a first charge over the property at the relevant time.
The secured creditor sought to enforce its security, and the governing secured-creditor regime had overriding effect over inconsistent laws.
issues.conclusion: The secured creditor’s dues had priority over the excise department’s dues in relation to the secured assets.
issues.legal_principle: The Crown’s preferential right to recover debts applies to unsecured creditors and does not displace a mortgagee, pledgee or other secured creditor. In the absence of a statutory first charge, secured claims prevail over government dues. The Court relied on Dena Bank v. Bhikhabhai Prabhu Dass Parikh, Central Bank of India v. Siriguppa Sugars & Chemicals Ltd., Union of India v. SICOM Ltd., and the Madras High Court’s reasoning in UTI Bank Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner, Central Excise, whose appeal was dismissed. The Court applied Sections 2(zc)–(zf), 13 and 35 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002; the later first-charge provision in Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 was itself subject to the secured-creditor statutes.

rule.if: priority_dispute_between_secured_creditor_and_tax_authority and creditor_holds_security_over_disputed_assets and tax_authority_claims_government_dues and no_applicable_tax_first_charge and secured_creditor_regime_overrides_inconsistent_law

predicates.priority_dispute_between_secured_credito: A proceeding concerns competing claims by a secured creditor and a government authority to recover from the same assets.
predicates.creditor_holds_security_over_disputed_as: A creditor holds a mortgage, charge, hypothecation or other security interest over the assets in dispute.
predicates.tax_authority_claims_government_dues: A government authority seeks payment of taxes, duties, penalties or other public dues from the debtor or its assets.
predicates.no_applicable_tax_first_charge: No applicable law gives the government dues a first charge over the disputed assets that prevails over the secured creditor’s claim.
predicates.secured_creditor_regime_overrides_incons: The governing secured-creditor regime gives the creditor priority and overrides inconsistent legal rules.
predicates.secured_creditor_has_priority: The secured creditor’s claim has priority over the government authority’s claim to the secured assets.

issues.definition: When a secured creditor and a government authority claim against the same assets, the secured creditor has priority if it holds security over those assets, no applicable tax first charge prevails, and the governing secured-creditor regime overrides inconsistent law.
